messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Destiny is a 19-year-old Native American woman who lives with her husband in a small apartment on the outskirts of a mid-sized city. She has been unemployed since the assault occurred approximately eight months ago, and she presents to the clinic visibly tense, her arms folded tightly across her body, her eyes moving frequently toward the door.

On a warm evening in early spring, Destiny had stepped outside a convenience store after buying a drink when a man she did not know approached her from behind. He smelled strongly of alcohol — she would later describe it as something sharp and sweet that she could not name — and within seconds had grabbed her and forced her into the narrow alley beside the building. Throughout the assault, he shouted at her in Arabic, a language she did not understand, and the words felt to her like an additional violation, incomprehensible and therefore boundless in their threat. The roar of a motorcycle passing on the street at some point during the attack became threaded into the experience in a way she cannot fully explain, only that the sound seemed to mark the moment she understood no one was coming to help her. She managed to break free and ran, but the man was never identified or apprehended.

In the weeks that followed, Destiny found that her body and the world around her had become unreliable in equal measure. A motorcycle accelerating on a nearby road could, without any transitional moment of recognition, return her entirely to the alley — not as a memory she was recalling but as something happening to her right then, her heart slamming, her breath gone. The smell of alcohol on a stranger's breath, or even passing a bar with its doors open, produced the same collapse of time. She began to hear, on certain days, fragments of shouted syllables in her mind, sounds she could not parse but that carried the full weight of that night. She could not predict when any of this would happen, and the unpredictability itself became its own source of dread.

She had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that the world she had understood before the assault — one in which strangers were mostly neutral, in which public spaces were navigable, in which she had some basic standing in her own life — no longer existed. What frightened her most was not any single trigger but the conclusion she had drawn: that the event had happened because she was the kind of person it could happen to, and that someone with more presence or strength or instinct would have stopped it before it reached that point. She returned to this thought often, turning it over without resolution.

Destiny stopped going outside after dark entirely. Her husband sometimes asked her to walk with him in the evenings, and she would decline without explanation, and the distance between them grew in ways neither of them named directly. She avoided the date on the calendar with a vigilance that surprised even her — rerouting her awareness around it for days on either side. She had also, gradually and without deciding to, stopped looking at herself in the mirror or paying attention to her own body in any deliberate way, as though her physical self had become a site she could not safely visit.

Inside the apartment, she listened. She was often positioned near walls, and she would register every sound at the door — footsteps in the hallway, the particular creak of the building settling — and assess each one before she could move on. When she did go out during daylight, she checked behind her repeatedly, certain on some level that the man, still unidentified, was capable of finding her.

She had not worked since the assault. She had previously taken pride in her independence and her plans, and she was certain now that the person who had held those plans no longer existed in any functional sense.

What finally brought her to seek help was a conversation with her husband in which he told her, gently, that he did not know how to reach her anymore. She came to the clinic not entirely sure what she was hoping for, but most afraid that what she had lost about herself was not recoverable.
